about: Which numeric datatypes each accelerator ARCHITECTURE accepts as a compute operand. VENDOR-PUBLISHED CAPABILITY FACTS ONLY -- this file records SUPPORT (a documented capability), never PERFORMANCE: no TOPS/TFLOPS, no clocks, no measured rates, no machine inventory. Rows are architectures, not products or machines. SCOPE: discrete and integrated GPUs, CPU SIMD/tile extensions, and accelerators in laptop/desktop/PCIe-card form. Accelerators embedded in phone- and SBC-class SoCs, and licensable DSP/NPU IP cores, are deliberately OUT of scope -- their operand lists are largely unpublished or NDA-walled, so those rows were mostly `unknown` and taught the reader little. Columns cover scalar floats, BLOCK-SCALED formats (a group of elements sharing one scale: MX = OCP microscaling with an E8M0 scale, NVFP4 = an e4m3 scale over a block of 16, BFP8/BFP4 = Tenstorrent block float), and integers. Consumed by the dtype-bits page's hardware-support view.
unknown_rule: `unknown` means the vendor does not publish the answer. It is a DISTINCT state from `none` and must render as unknown -- never collapse it to a guess, a default, or a `none`. `none` is used only where a vendor enumerates a complete operand list that omits the dtype, or where the architecture has no engine that could accept it. A vendor's TOOLCHAIN accepting a dtype is not the same claim as its ENGINE multiplying in that dtype; where a vendor's own documents blur the two, the note says which one the level records. TWO KINDS OF UNKNOWN, and the note says which: (a) the vendor publishes NOTHING on this dtype for this engine -- there is no enumeration for it to be absent from; and (b) the vendor DOES document it but only behind a login or an NDA, so the answer exists and is not disclosable. (b) is not a gap anyone can close by looking harder, and saying so is more useful to a reader than an unqualified shrug. An `unknown` whose note gives no reason at all is an incomplete cell, not a finished one.

levels.native: Documented native operand of the architecture's MATRIX / tensor engine.
levels.vector: Documented native operand of the vector / SIMD / scalar ALU only -- there is no matrix engine, or the matrix engine does not take this dtype.
levels.emulated: Reachable only by converting (upconverting / decompressing) to a wider type the hardware does accept.
levels.none: Documented as not supported by this architecture -- including the common case where a vendor toolchain ACCEPTS a wider dtype and then executes it at a narrower one (fp32 in, fp16 math): the engine has no path for it. `emulated` is the opposite direction, a narrow dtype WIDENED to something the hardware accepts.
levels.unknown: Not publicly documented by the vendor.

classes.gpu-matrix: GPU with a dedicated matrix/tensor engine (Tensor Core, WMMA, XMX/DPAS).
classes.gpu-alu: GPU with no matrix engine -- GEMM is emitted as vector/scalar FMA and integer dot products.
classes.npu: Fixed-function neural accelerator or AI ASIC.
classes.cpu-simd: CPU SIMD/vector ISA path (and, where present, a CPU tile-matrix unit).

fp64.note: The CUDA-core double-precision path is present at a small fraction of the fp32 rate so that fp64 programs run correctly; the FP64 TENSOR CORE is a datacenter-part feature and is not on this die.

fp32.note: CUDA-core FMA operand and the Tensor Core ACCUMULATOR type; TF32 is the 32-bit-range format the tensor engine actually ingests.

tf32.note: TF32 is the tensor core's 32-bit-RANGE operand -- fp32's 8 exponent bits with fp16's 10 mantissa bits -- introduced on Ampere and still an `mma` input here.

fp16.note: The original tensor-core operand, and still the default one: fp16 x fp16 accumulating into fp32.

bf16.note: Same tensor-core shape as fp16, fp32's exponent range with a shorter mantissa -- which is why training and quantized-weight paths prefer it over fp16.

fp8e4m3.note: OCP FP8; also the element type inside the NVFP4/MXFP8 block-scaled forms.

fp8e5m2.note: The IEEE-shaped 8-bit float, with Inf and NaN and one fewer mantissa bit than e4m3. Both fp8 encodings are tensor-core operands from Ada on.

fp6e3m2.note: A 6-bit FLOAT tensor operand in its own right: the `kind::f8f6f4` mma family takes e3m2 unscaled, and the same operand appears block-scaled inside MXFP6. This is the generation that made sub-8-bit float a hardware operand.

fp6e2m3.note: The second OCP 6-bit encoding -- one more mantissa bit, one less exponent bit than e3m2. Same `kind::f8f6f4` mma family, unscaled or block-scaled.

fp4e2m1.note: The 4-bit float this generation is marketed on -- an mma input type in its own right (unscaled, via the `kind::f8f6f4` family) and the element type inside both MXFP4 and NVFP4. Contrast the 4-bit INTEGER operand on the same row, which this generation dropped.

mxfp8.note: OCP microscaling: a block of fp8 elements sharing one E8M0 (power-of-two) scale, consumed by the block-scaled `mma` forms.

mxfp6.note: OCP microscaling over 6-bit float elements -- same block-scaled `mma` family as MXFP8, same E8M0 shared scale.

mxfp4.note: OCP microscaling over e2m1 elements with an E8M0 shared scale; PTX gives it its own `mma` kind.

nvfp4.note: NVIDIA's own 4-bit block format: e2m1 elements in blocks of 16 with an e4m3 (not power-of-two) shared scale, which is exactly why it is a separate `mma` operand kind from MXFP4.

bfp8.note: BFP8 / BFP4 are Tenstorrent's own block-float tile formats -- a block of values sharing one exponent -- and appear in no other vendor's operand list.

int32.note: 32-bit integer multiply is a CUDA-core instruction. For the tensor core int32 is the ACCUMULATOR the 8-bit and 4-bit forms write into, never an input.

int16.note: PTX defines 16-bit integer arithmetic on the CUDA cores, and it is not in the tensor core's input-type table. NVIDIA does not publish how wide the underlying integer datapath is.

int8.note: The quantized-inference workhorse: int8 x int8 accumulating into int32, with the unsigned and mixed-sign forms as separate documented stems.

uint8.note: `mma` documents u8 operands alongside s8, including the mixed s8xu8 shapes.

int4.note: Blackwell DROPPED the sub-byte integer tensor operand its two predecessors had. The PTX form still assembles, but it is no longer an instruction: the assembler lowers it to a software helper of ~200 instructions of which only TWO touch the tensor core -- the rest is bit-unpacking and sign-extension on the integer ALU. On the previous two generations the identical source compiles to ONE 4-bit tensor instruction. Run on the silicon it is numerically exact (and bit-identical to doing the same work as two 8-bit tensor ops by hand), just far slower than the 8-bit path it appears to undercut. So a 4-bit INTEGER here is a compatibility shim, not a fast path -- the 4-bit path this generation actually added is FLOAT (fp4 e2m1, MXFP4, NVFP4).

int2.note: No NVIDIA generation has ever defined a 2-bit tensor operand: the integer `mma` stems are s8/u8, s4/u4 (through Ada) and b1 (through Ada). 2-bit weights are unpacked before they reach the engine. Reachable only by widening: 2-bit values are unpacked into int8 lanes -- this row's 8-bit matrix operand -- before they are multiplied, so the unpack, not the multiply, sets the rate. Narrower storage still cuts weight bytes, which is the win on a bandwidth-bound decode; it is not an arithmetic win.

int1.note: The binary tensor operand -- bitwise AND for the multiply, population count for the reduction -- that Ampere and Ada implement as ONE instruction is gone here. Like the 4-bit integer it lowers to a software helper, this one issuing EIGHT 8-bit tensor ops plus the bit-shuffling around them; it computes the right answer on the device and is slower than the 8-bit path. The helper's name marks where the removal happened: it is shared with the datacenter Blackwell target, not with any earlier one.

One caveat if you go looking for it: the high-level host API refuses tf32 outright (its size helpers raise "TF32 unsupported atm"), so it is reachable at the low-level compute layer while the SDK surface above it does not expose it. fp16.note: An fp16 x fp16 source pair accumulating into fp32 or fp16 -- though the user-facing tensor API exposes bf16 rather than fp16.

fp8e4m3.note: Storage-only, exactly like the e5m2 encoding beside it -- and on this silicon e4m3 is not even a separate hardware code point: it is the e5m2 code point plus a mode bit that reinterprets the exponent width. Either way the unpacker widens it to fp16 before the math unit sees it, so both 8-bit floats buy bandwidth and neither buys arithmetic.

fp8e5m2.note: Settled from the open compute stack, and it is the SAME answer as e4m3. The vendor's name for this encoding is not an OCP-style one, which is why it looks unresolved at first glance: their 8-bit float format is documented as "FP8, e5m2", and the next-generation headers rename the same enum value while stating the encoding outright. It is a real L1/tile storage format on both parts -- but the UNPACKER converts it to fp16 on the way into the source registers, and the stack says so plainly: the hardware always produces fp16 data in the register. The math unit never multiplies fp8. Storage density, not arithmetic.

architectures.source: Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile (FEAT_I8MM, FEAT_BF16)

fp64.note: AArch64 Advanced SIMD carries a packed pair of doubles; fp64 is a baseline element size.

fp32.note: fp32 is the accumulator for every NEON matrix instruction, never a multiplicand: fp32 matrix multiply exists only in SVE, not in Advanced SIMD, at any feature level.

tf32.note: No Arm feature defines a tf32 operand.

fp16.note: Native half-precision SIMD arithmetic, not merely half-precision storage: this feature level computes in fp16 rather than converting to fp32 first. Separate from the 8-bit matrix instructions that give this row its name.

bf16.note: BFMMLA multiplies a 2x4 by a 4x2 bf16 block into a 2x2 fp32 accumulator -- a matrix instruction on a CPU. BFDOT gives the same operand type a plain 2-wide dot into fp32.

fp8e4m3.note: FP8 reaches the A-profile architecture later (Armv9.2), as its own feature set with its own matrix instructions. Reachable only by widening: a fp8 e4m3 value is converted to fp16 -- this row's vector path -- before anything multiplies it. The data survives; the engine never sees the format, and the convert/repack cost per element does not shrink with the format, so the narrower encoding buys storage and bandwidth rather than arithmetic.
